results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You should keep your tax records for as long as the Internal Revenue Code allows you to amend a return or the IRS can assess additional tax—this is called the “period of limitations.” Keep a copy of every filed return and all supporting documents until that period expires [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  

**Specific rules that tell you how long to keep particular records**

| Type of record | Minimum retention period | Source |
|----------------|--------------------------|--------|
| General income‑and‑deduction records | Until the period of limitations for that return “runs out” – usually the time the IRS can amend the return or assess tax (generally up to 3 years after the return is filed, but it can be longer for certain situations). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Copies of filed returns | Keep indefinitely, because they help prepare future returns and support any audit. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., payroll, Forms 941, 940, W‑2s, W‑3s, 1099s) | At least **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid** (whichever is later). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (depreciation, amortization, basis, sale of property) | Until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Refund‑claim records | If you file a refund claim, you must file it **within 3 years from the date you filed the original return** or **2 years from the date the tax was paid**, whichever is later. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49) |

**Bottom line**  
- Keep most tax records (income, deductions, receipts, etc.) until the IRS’s period of limitations for that tax year expires.  
- Keep employment‑tax records for 4 years after they are due or paid.  
- Keep asset records for the same length of time as needed to calculate depreciation or calculate gain/loss when sold.  
- Store copies of all filed returns permanently.  
- File any refund claims within the time limits listed above.

These guidelines should satisfy the IRS’s retention requirements and give you the documentation you’ll need for future returns or audits.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 49)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several essential purposes:

1. **Monitor the progress of your business** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, or what changes are needed. This can increase the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Records are required to produce income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which help you manage the business and deal with banks or creditors. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Identify the source of receipts** – Knowing where money or property comes from helps separate business from non‑business receipts and distinguishes taxable from non‑taxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Track deductible expenses** – Recording expenses when they occur ensures you don’t forget them when filing tax returns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Prepare tax returns** – The same records that monitor the business and produce financial statements must also support the income, expenses, and credits reported on your tax return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **Support items reported on tax returns** – Keeping records available at all times allows the IRS to inspect them if an examination occurs, and a complete set speeds up the process. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

In short, keeping records lets you manage the business effectively, meet tax‑reporting obligations, and defend your filings if the IRS reviews them.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
You can choose any of the methods listed in the IRS guidance, but the best choice depends on how your business records income and expenses and whether you keep inventory.  
Here’s what the IRS says you can use and how to decide between them:

| Accounting method | When it’s reported | When expenses are deductible | Typical business situations |
|-------------------|---------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Cash method** | Income is recorded as it is received. | Expenses are deducted (or capitalized) when they are paid. | Good for small, service‑only businesses that don’t carry inventory or have simple cash flows.  |
| **Accrual method** | Income is recorded when earned, even if payment comes later. | Expenses are deducted (or capitalized) when incurred, regardless of when you pay them. | Needed for businesses that sell inventory or have significant receivables/payables; matches income with related expenses.  |
| **Special methods** | Specific rules for items such as bad‑debts, depreciation, depletion, installment sales, or long‑term contracts. | Follow the separate rules for each item. | Use when your business has those specific accounting needs.  |
| **Combination method** | Mix of the above, but must act like the method that shows your income. | If you include cash items, the combination is treated as a cash method; if you include accrual items, it’s treated as accrual. | Use when you need to combine a cash approach for some items (e.g., payroll) with accrual for others (e.g., inventory).  |

**Key rules that guide your choice**

* **Inventory requirement** – If you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise you must keep inventory and use an accrual method for purchases and sales.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
* **Consistency** – Once you pick a method, you must use it consistently for all income and expenses; if you change it later you need IRS approval via Form 3115. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  
* **Choosing at first filing** – The method is chosen when you file your first income‑tax return that includes Schedule C (Form 1040). After that, a change requires IRS approval. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
* **Special situations** – If you have separate businesses you can use different methods for each, as long as you keep separate books. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**How to decide**

1. **Do you hold inventory?**  
   * Yes → use accrual (or a combination that includes accrual for inventory).  
   * No → you may use cash or a cash‑based combination.

2. **Do you have significant receivables or payables?**  
   * Yes → accrual better matches income to the period earned.  
   * No → cash may be simpler.

3. **Do you need special treatments (depreciation, bad debts, etc.)?**  
   * Yes → include those special methods; they can be combined with either cash or accrual.  

4. **How complex do you want your bookkeeping to be?**  
   * Simple cash system is easier for very small or new businesses.  
   * Double‑entry accrual systems give more accurate long‑term financial pictures.  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=28)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=29)  

**Bottom line**

- **Cash method** if you’re a small, service‑only business with no inventory and want the simplest reporting.  
- **Accrual method** if you sell inventory, track receivables, or need to match income with related expenses.  
- **Special or combination methods** if your business has unique accounting needs or you want aspects of both cash and accrual.  

You decide when you file your first return and can change only with IRS approval.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
Check your workplace for hazards by following the step‑by‑step approach the handbook recommends:

1. Conduct routine **self‑inspections** – have knowledgeable workers walk the site and look for obvious dangers such as blocked exits, wet spots, or exposed wiring.  
   ➜ “Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to: identify hazards; control identified hazards; and monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. Use the **handbook’s self‑inspection checklists** as a starting point. These checklists cover general industry workplaces (excluding construction or maritime) and help you see where to begin fixing problems.  
   ➜ “The checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces... They are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. Compile the data you gather from the checklists with records you already keep—injury/illness logs, worker training records, maintenance logs, and incident reports. This combined picture shows where the biggest problems lie.  
   ➜ “Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information… to help you determine where challenges exist.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. After you spot a hazard, read the relevant **OSHA standard** to understand what the law requires for that situation, and then decide how to control it. The handbook advises reviewing each applicable standard and, if unsure, contacting OSHA or a local On‑Site Consultation program.  
   ➜ “Review the OSHA standards to identify those that apply to your business… If you have any questions… visit the OSHA website or contact the nearest OSHA Area Office.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. Incorporate inspections into your everyday safety routine. Treat them as part of your daily business operations, and keep records of any corrective actions taken.  
   ➜ “Regular workplace inspections are an important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

By doing this monthly (or as often as your business size and hazards warrant), you’ll constantly spot new risks, verify that existing controls still work, and keep the workplace safer.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash‑method accounting vs. accrual‑method accounting – the key difference is **when** you report income and expenses.

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is counted** | When you actually receive the money (or when it is constructively received, e.g., credited to your account) | When you earn it – when the performance is complete or the sale is made, even if you don’t receive payment until later |
| **When expenses are deducted or capitalized** | When you pay the money | When the expense is incurred – when you receive the goods or services, regardless of payment date |
| **Inventory rule** | If you keep inventory for sales, you *must* use the accrual method for purchases and sales, but can still use cash for other items | Must use accrual for all inventory‑related transactions |
| **Combination method** | You may mix cash and accrual for different items only if it “clearly” shows income and is used consistently; if the combination includes cash, you are treated as using cash for all reporting | If you choose accrual for any part, you must use accrual for all income and expenses |
| **Typical users** | Sole proprietors with no inventory, small businesses for simplicity | Businesses with inventory, larger firms, or those needing better matching of income and expenses |

**Why it matters**

*Under cash*: If a client sends you a check on December 30, 2024 and you receive it on January 4, 2025, you include that $⨉ in 2025 income ([[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)).

*Under accrual*: If you sell a computer on December 28, 2025 but bill in January 2026 and receive payment in February 2026, you still include the income in 2025 because that is when you earned it ([[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)).

**Practical tip**  
If your business has inventory (goods held for sale, raw materials that become part of merchandise), you must use the accrual method for those transactions even if you otherwise use cash for most things ([[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)).

In short, choose cash when you want to match income with cash actually received and expenses with cash actually paid. Choose accrual when you want to match income and expenses in the period they occur, which is generally required for businesses that carry inventory.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary should be concise—usually one or two paragraphs—and give the reader a clear, high‑level snapshot of the business plan. It should

* Briefly describe the business idea  
* State how much money is needed, what it will be used for, and how much has already been invested  
* Provide a short schedule of goals or milestones  

Because many details are only known after the rest of the plan is written, it is best to write the executive summary last. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, spell out who your best customers are and what defines them. Here’s how to structure that section, drawing directly from the guidance in the plan:

- **Define the market niche**: State the specific segment of the market you will serve. This could be a Business‑to‑Business (B‑2‑B) niche (e.g., HVAC service for mid‑size office buildings) or a Business‑to‑Consumer (B‑2‑C) niche (e.g., gluten‑free baked goods for health‑conscious adults). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

- **Identify the best customer**: Describe the ideal buyer by listing key characteristics such as industry, company size, and location for B‑2‑B, or age, gender, income level, lifestyle, and buying motives for B‑2‑C. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

- **Segment the market**: Explain how you’ve broken the overall market into meaningful groups—by demographics (age, gender), geography (city, region), economic status, or product use/application. Mention any specific sub‑segments that are most attractive. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

- **Estimate size and growth**: Provide rough population figures, sales tax data, or industry reports to estimate the total addressable market, as well as the portion you expect to capture. Note projected growth trends that justify the opportunity. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

- **Illustrate with examples**: Give concrete examples of the types of customers you’ll target, such as “small businesses with 5–20 employees in the Northeast corridor looking for cost‑effective cleaning services.”  Use these examples throughout to clarify who you’re aiming to attract. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  
If you own or operate a business that serves the public, you are required by the ADA to remove any physical “barriers” that are **readily achievable** so that the business is accessible to people with disabilities, including those who use wheelchairs.  This means providing a clear, accessible entrance and route, clear floor spaces in front of counters, and other accessibility features that can be reasonably implemented.  If something is not readily achievable, you must provide an alternative means of access or service.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) states, “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical ‘barriers’ that are ‘readily achievable’…”  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) adds that when a shop cannot provide an accessible entrance, it must provide an alternative accessible route or entrance and display a sign directing people to it.  

Therefore, unless the required changes are impossible or would impose excessive cost, you must make your shop wheelchair‑accessible.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You may be exempt from OSHA’s injury‑recordkeeping rules **only** if you meet one of these two conditions:

1. **Small employer** – you had **10 or fewer workers for the entire last calendar year** (29 CFR 1904.1).  
2. **Low‑hazard industry** – your business is listed in **29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A** as a low‑hazard industry.  

If either of those applies, you do **not** need to keep OSHA Forms 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) or 301 (Incident Report), but you still must:

* Record **all work‑related fatalities**.  
* Report **in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA.  

(These reporting requirements apply to every employer, regardless of size or industry.)  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

If you do **not** meet either exemption, you must:

* Keep a record of every occupational injury or illness, except minor injuries that require only first aid, on OSHA Form 300.  
* Prepare a supplementary record (OSHA Form 301) for each recordable case.  
* Summarize the year’s data on OSHA Form 300A.  

Employment records (injury/illness logs, Form 301, and Form 300A) must be kept at the worksite for at least **five years**.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

**Bottom line:** Check the size of your workforce and the hazard classification of your industry. If you meet the exemption criteria, you’re exempt from the detailed injury recordkeeping but must still report major incidents. If you don’t meet those criteria, you must keep the full OSHA record‑keeping set.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax‑record keeping**

| What you need to keep | How long to keep it | Source |
|------------------------|---------------------|--------|
| All records that support an item of income or deduction on a return (receipts, invoices, bank statements, etc.) | Keep them for the period of limitations that applies to the return – the time during which you can amend the return or the IRS can assess additional tax.  §1.1 of the Internal Revenue Code [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |  
| Copies of filed tax returns | Keep these copies indefinitely; they help when you prepare future returns or file an amended return.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |  
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., payroll, W‑2s, Forms 941/944, etc.) | Keep them **at least 4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid (whichever is later).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |  
| Asset‑related records (depreciation schedules, basis statements, disposition documents) | Keep them until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |  
| Electronic versions of hard‑copy books and records | Must be retained **as long as they are material to the administration of tax law** – essentially the same period as the hard copies.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

**Injury/OSHA‑record keeping**

| What you need to keep | How long to keep it | Source |
|-----------------------|---------------------|--------|
| OSHA Form 300 (Log of work‑related injuries and illnesses), Form 301 (Incident report), and the annual Form 300A (Summary of injuries and illnesses) | **Keep at the worksite for at least 5 years** after the end of the calendar year covered by the records.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |  
| Worker medical records and exposure records | Retain **for the time period required for each specific type of record** (e.g., medical records for the duration of each medical condition).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |  
| Worker training records (e.g., safety or first‑aid training) | Keep accessible for review by workers; retention period is the time required by OSHA standards.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |  
| All work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye | Must be reported to OSHA within 8 / 24 hours and retained as part of the 5‑year period above.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |  
| Electronic submission of OSHA logs | If you have an establishment with ≥ 100 workers in a high‑hazard industry, electronically submit OSHA Form 300 and Form 301 **by March 2** of the year following the calendar year covered.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |  

**Summary**

*Keep all taxpayer‑supporting documents for the period that the tax law allows you to modify the return or for which the IRS can assess tax (generally 4 years for employment‑tax records).*  
*Record all work‑related injuries and illnesses on OSHA forms and keep them at the site for at least five years, plus any additional medical or training records for the time required by OSHA or other applicable regulations.*  

These retention times are those explicitly stated in the provided sources; if you need to retain records for a longer period (e.g., due to specific claims or audits), the IRS or OSHA may allow extensions.

• Review the program at least annually and update it when new hazards appear. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6) | | **Involve employees** in safety planning. | • Hold regular safety meetings or “huddles.”

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Is there a specific answer in the provided material?**  
Yes – the segments include detailed instructions for writing a business plan and for establishing an accounting system.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that pulls in every relevant piece of information from the segments.

---

## 1. Writing a Business Plan  

A complete business plan is organized into clear sections. Use the sections and sub‑headings outlined in the segments so that your plan stays consistent and covers everything lenders, investors, and partners expect.

| Section | What to Include | Source |
|--------|-----------------|--------|
| **Cover Page** | Company name, address, phone, owners’ names & contacts, date, logo | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Table of Contents** | Optional, but useful for long plans | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Executive Summary** | One‑to‑two paragraph snapshot: business idea, funds needed, current investment, and timeline | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Company Description** | Industry overview, competitive edge, business history, growth outlook | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Products / Services** | Detailed product/service description, market need, unique selling points, future offerings | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Proprietary Information** | Patents, copyrights, trademarks, other IP protection | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Regulations** | Licenses, permits, state/local agencies, compliance status | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Facility & Equipment** | Location, building details, equipment needs, future scalability | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Market Analysis** | Target market, size, trends, competition, differentiation | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15) |
| **Marketing & Sales** | Promotion strategy, distribution channels, sales tactics | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15) |
| **Operations Plan** | Daily operations, staffing, suppliers, quality control | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Management & Organization** | Legal structure, owners, board, day‑to‑day managers, qualifications | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13) |
| **Human Resources** | Employee numbers, job titles, responsibilities, wages, benefits | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13) |
| **Financial Plan** | 3‑year financial projections (income statement, cash flow, balance sheet), capital requirements, equity | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) |
| **Appendices** | Licenses, leases, contracts, credit reports, supporting documents | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17) |

**Tip** – If you need help refining numbers, the South Dakota Small Business Development Center offers free consulting on financial projections; contact the nearest office listed in Segment 32.

---

## 2. Setting Up Accounting  

### 2.1 Choose a Business Structure & Obtain IDs  
| Step | Detail | Source |
|------|--------|--------|
| 1 | Pick legal form (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC). The choice affects tax forms, liability, and bookkeeping | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |
| 2 | Obtain a Federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you’ll hire employees or prefer a separate tax ID | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |
| 3 | If the business uses a name other than owners’ names, file a fictitious name statement (for South Dakota) | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |
| 4 | If incorporated or forming an LLC, file articles with the Secretary of State | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |

### 2.2 Open a Dedicated Business Checking Account  
- Keep business funds separate from personal funds.  
- Record deposits with source tags (income, personal funds, loans).  
- Use checks that are payable to vendors or “cash” only for business expenses. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

### 2.3 Record Every Transaction Promptly  
- **Daily**: Log receipts, deposits, and disbursements.  
- **Weekly / Monthly**: Summarize cash receipts and disbursements. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14), [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

### 2.4 Pick an Accounting Method  
| Method | Best For | Consistency Requirement | Source |
|--------|----------|-----------------------|--------|
| Cash | Small businesses; expenses recorded when paid | Must match tax return and books | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Accrual | Companies that keep inventory or have receivables | Must use consistently, match tax return | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Combination | Uses cash for personal items, accrual for business income | Treat each segment consistently | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |

- **Rule**: Your accounting method must appear on the first tax return (e.g., Schedule C for sole proprietors). If you change later, file Form 3115 for IRS approval. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16), [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

### 2.5 Set Up Books (Single‑Entry vs. Double‑Entry)  

| System | How It Works | When to Use |
|--------|--------------|-------------|
| Single‑Entry | Only income statement style; record daily cash receipts and monthly summaries | Small sole‑prop businesses with simple cash flows | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Double‑Entry | Journals ➜ Ledgers ➜ Balance sheet | Any business that needs asset/liability tracking | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |

- **Journals** log each transaction.  
- **Ledgers** aggregate accounts: Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Income, Expenses.  

### 2.6 Keep Supporting Records  
- Deposit slips, withdrawal slips, invoices, receipts, credit‑card sales slips, checkbooks.  
- Electronic records must be indexed, preserve, recoverable, and readable. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12), [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

### 2.7 Reconcile Frequently  
- Compare bank statements to checkbook and accounting records; rectify differences immediately. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

### 2.8 Prepare and Store Financial Statements  
- **Income Statement** (profit & loss)  
- **Cash Flow Statement** – 3‑year outlook at month‑level  
- **Balance Sheet** – snapshot of assets, liabilities, equity  

These documents are part of the “Money” section of a business plan and also required for tax filings and lender requests. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) |

### 2.9 Regular Tax and Payroll Reporting (if applicable)  
- File Forms W‑2, W‑3, 1099‑MISC

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you:  
* Pay wages to one or more employees, or  
* File pension or excise tax returns.  

A sole‑prop business that has no employees may also obtain an EIN if it prefers to use a business TIN instead of its owner’s Social Security number.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6).

**What accounting method comes with it?**  
An EIN does not dictate an accounting method.  When you file your first income‑tax return (for example, a Schedule C on Form 1040), you must choose an accounting method.  The two basic options are:  

1. **Cash method** – report income when received and expenses when paid.  
2. **Accrual method** – report income when earned and expenses when incurred.  

You may also use special or combination methods as allowed, but the choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
The OSHA injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules say you must keep the following documents:

| Form | What it covers | How long you must keep it |
|------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | Records of each work‑related injury or illness that is *recordable* (i.e., requires an incident report). | At least **five years** at the worksite. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | A detailed incident report for each recordable injury or illness. | At least **five years** at the worksite. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | An annual summary of all Form 300 and 301 entries. | At least **five years** at the worksite (the same period as the individual logs). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

*Optional:* Many employers also create their own equivalent forms that contain the same required information as Form 301, and they can keep those for the same period.

**Key points**

- The requirement applies to all employers that are *not* exempt under 29 CFR 1904.1 (those with 10 or fewer workers or in certain low‑hazard industries). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- The records must be kept at the workplace; they do **not** need to be filed with OSHA unless the employer has a high‑hazard industry with 100+ workers, in which case the logs must be submitted electronically by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- The five‑year rule applies to the records themselves; the employer must keep the records for at least that long. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

**In short:** keep OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A (or equivalent forms) and retain them for a minimum of five years.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
results.answer:
You must file a few federal employment‑tax forms and keep certain employee records:

* **Quarterly/annual federal payroll reports** – Use **Form 941 (Quarterly)** or **Form 944 (Annual)** to report Social Security, Medicare and federal income‑tax withholding. For farms use Form 943. These are the forms that carry the totals of the taxes you and your employees owe. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
* **Federal unemployment (FUTA) tax** – Report and pay FUTA on **Form 940 (Annual)**. Employees do not contribute to this tax; it is paid entirely by you. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
* **Year‑end employee statements** – Issue **Form W‑2** to each employee to report wages, tips, and the amounts withheld for federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
* **Employee eligibility** – Have each new employee complete **Form I‑9** (employment‑eligibility verification). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
* **Employee withholding election** – Collect each employee’s **Form W‑4** so you can withhold the correct amount of federal income tax. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)

The provided segments do not state which state taxes you must withhold or pay on behalf of your employees, nor do they give specific deadlines or the exact forms required for state withholding, state unemployment insurance, or other state payroll taxes. Therefore that part of the question is not answered by the given information.

**Summary of required federal filings (per the segments):**  
- Form 941 or 944 (employer’s quarterly/annual federal tax return) – Social Security, Medicare, income‑tax withholding.

results.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
results.answer:
**If a customer can’t get through your front door**

- Make the entrance physically accessible or give a sign that points customers to an alternative entrance that is accessible.  
  - Doors should be at least 36 in. wide (or 32 in. if a 36‑in. width can’t be achieved) and any hardware that requires a tight grasp (round doorknob, panel‑type handle, thumb latch) should be replaced or modified with a lever‑type handle or a clamp‑on lever. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
  - If the main entrance cannot be made accessible, a sign must be posted that directs customers to a nearby accessible entrance, and that alternative entrance must remain open during business hours. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

**If someone is hurt on site**

1. **Medical services / first aid**  
   - Provide immediate post‑exposure medical evaluation for any blood‑borne‑pathogen exposure.  
   - Post emergency phone numbers and keep them easily reachable. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=63)

2. **Recordkeeping**  
   - Report injuries or illnesses that are not minor first‑aid cases on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
   - For each recordable case, prepare a Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report).  
   - Annually summarize all recordable incidents on OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
   - Employers with 10 or fewer workers or in certain low‑hazard industries may be exempt from the detailed recordkeeping, but all work‑related fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye must still be reported to OSHA. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

3. **Hazard identification and reporting**  
   - A procedure must exist for workers to report injuries, illnesses, incidents (including near‑misses), hazards, and safety concerns.  
   - Workers must be trained to identify and control hazards. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)  

4. **Emergency preparedness**  
   - Ensure that exit doors are unobstructed, panic hardware allows the door to open with ≤15 lb force, and that exit paths are clearly marked and adequately lit. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23)  
   - Maintain a buddy system, have clear instructions for calling emergency services, and post heat‑related or other emergency procedures as needed. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=43)  

In short, make the door usable or provide an alternate accessible route, and when an injury occurs, treat it promptly, record it, and follow OSHA’s reporting and hazard‑control procedures.

results.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
results.answer:
The answer is covered in the segments below.

**Cash reporting threshold**  
You must file Form 8300 and report any cash payments that total more than **$10,000** in a single transaction or in two or more related business transactions. “Cash includes U.S. and foreign coin and currency. It also includes certain monetary instruments such as cashier’s and traveler’s checks and money orders” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12). The same requirement appears again in Segment 4, confirming the $10,000 threshold for Form 8300 filing [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9).

**License to serve food**  
If you are preparing and serving food, “an inspection must be completed. Approval from the Health Department is needed before a food license or lodging license is issued” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8). So you do need a food license issued by the local Health Department, and you must have a health‑department inspection completed first.

**Summary**  
- Report cash receipts over **$10,000** with Form 8300.  
- Obtain a food license (after a health‑department inspection) before serving food.

results.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
results.answer:
**Why you should have a safety program**

1. A safety program is a proactive way to identify and fix hazards before they cause injury or illness. This prevents the loss of workers, families, and money, and keeps the business running smoothly.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
2. Investing in safety now can avoid costly losses later, making a safe business a “sound business.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  
3. A program shows you are in good faith and committed to protecting employees, which is required by OSHA and can help you avoid penalties or inspections. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

**Records you must keep**

| Type of record | What to keep | Length of retention or reporting deadline | Sources |
|----------------|--------------|------------------------------------------|---------|
| **Injury and illness log (OSHA Form 300)** | All recordable injuries or illnesses, except minor first‑aid cases | Keep on site for at least **5 years** | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Injury and illness incident report (OSHA Form 301)** | Detailed description of each recordable case | Keep with the 300 log at least **5 years** | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Annual summary (OSHA Form 300A)** | Summary of the year’s injuries and illnesses | Prepare each calendar year; used to report to OSHA | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Fatality, in‑patient hospitalization, amputation, loss of eye reports** | Must be reported to OSHA **within 8 hours** for fatalities and **within 24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, or eye loss | Report immediately, then keep records per OSHA rules | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical & exposure records** | Retain for the period required by the specific record type or by law | Retain for the required period for each record type | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Records of safety training given to employees | Keep accessible for review by workers; retain as required by OSHA standards | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Optional: OSHA Forms 300, 301, 300A for small businesses with ≤10 workers or in low‑hazard industries** | Employers with 10 or fewer workers may be exempt from recordkeeping unless in certain low‑hazard industries | If exempt, no records required; otherwise keep as above | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

These records prove that your business is following the OSHA requirements and help you monitor the safety program’s effectiveness.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
The IRS requires you to keep tax‑related records for the period that the law permits you to amend a return or that the IRS can assess additional tax.  Refer to **Segment 1**:

- **General tax records**: Keep any documents that support an item of income or a deduction “until the period of limitations for that return runs out” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).
- **Employment tax records**: If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).
- **Asset records**: Keep records related to property “until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).
- **Filed returns**: Keep copies of the tax returns you file because they help with future returns and are useful if the IRS revisits any item. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

If you need the exact limitation periods (e.g., 3 years for most returns, 7 years if you’ll claim bad‑debt or tax‑debt deductions, etc.), those specifics are listed in the table of limitation periods in the same section (Table 3), which is referenced but not printed here. Nonetheless, the rule per the IRS is to retain records until the relevant limitation period ends.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

* **Track the business’s performance** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which products are selling, and what changes may be necessary. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare financial statements** – Records are required to build income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which show income, expenses, assets, liabilities, and equity. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Identify the source of receipts** – Knowing where money or property comes from helps you separate business from non‑business receipts and taxable from nontaxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Track deductible expenses** – Recording expenses as they occur prevents you from forgetting deductible costs when you file your taxes. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare tax returns** – The same records you use for monitoring and financial statements also support the income, expenses, and credits reported on your tax returns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Support tax‑return items** – When the IRS reviews a return, you must provide records that back up what you report. Keeping a complete set of records speeds up any examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

In short, keeping business records lets you manage, grow, and report your business reliably while meeting the IRS’s documentation requirements.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
If you’re deciding between the two common accounting methods, the IRS guidance in the segments says:

* **Cash method** – You report income when you receive it and, usually, deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them.  
  *Use this method if you do **not** need to keep an inventory.*  

  *“You report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

* **Accrual method** – You report income in the year you earn it and expenses in the year you incur them, whether or not you get paid or actually pay that year.  

  *“Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it … You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

* **Inventory rule** – If your business holds inventory (goods for sale, raw materials, supplies that become part of merchandise), you **must use the accrual method** for purchases and sales.  

  *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales of merchandise.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
  *“If you use a combination method that includes the cash method… treat that combination method as the cash method.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

* **Combination method** – You may combine cash, accrual, or special methods, but the combination must clearly show income and expenses, and the inventory rule still applies. If you mix cash and accrual for different items, the overall method is treated as the cash method.  

  *“You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods… but… If you use a combination method that includes the cash method, treat that combination method as the cash method.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**Bottom line from the segments:**  
- Use the **cash method** if you do not hold inventory.  
- Use the **accrual method** if you do hold inventory (or need to record accruals for purchases/sales).  
- Combination methods are allowed but must follow the restrictions above.  

When you file your first tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040), you choose the method, and thereafter you must obtain IRS approval (Form 3115) to change it. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
**How to check your workplace for hazards**

1. **Do a routine self‑inspection** – The handbook explains that the only reliable way to know if hazards exist and are under control is to assess work processes directly. Small‑business employers are encouraged to carry out routine workplace self‑inspections to identify hazards, control them, and verify that the controls stay effective. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklists** – The hand‑book provides general‑industry checklists that serve as a starting point for spotting hazards. They are based on OSHA standards and accepted safety principles and can help you decide where to begin making the business safer. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Compile the checklist results with other data** – After you finish a checklist, combine the information with injury and illness records, training records, maintenance logs, and incident reports. This combined view helps you spot recurring problems and prioritize actions. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Keep your safety program alive** – Make the inspection part of a broader safety and health program: discuss safety with workers, let them report hazards, involve them in choosing controls, and record the outcomes. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

5. **Tap free resources** – If you want extra help, OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program offers no‑cost, confidential visits from trained safety professionals who can guide you through a thorough hazard assessment and suggest improvements. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

6. **Make safety part of daily work** – The handbook stresses that regular inspections are an important tool for identifying and fixing hazards, and that safety should be woven into everyday business operations rather than treated as an add‑on. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

**In short:**  
Plan regular inspections → use the supplied checklists → log the findings with other workplace records → involve workers in control decisions → use free OSHA resources when needed. This systematic approach lets you spot hazards early, put controls in place, and keep your workplace safer.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
**Cash vs. accrual accounting – the key difference**

| Accounting method | When you record income | When you record expenses | Why it matters |
|-------------------|------------------------|--------------------------|----------------|
| **Cash method** | In the year you *receive* the money (or it becomes constructively available to you). | In the year you *pay* the money (or it becomes constructively payable). | It matches cash flow: you only report money that actually moves into or out of your bank account. |
| **Accrual method** | In the year you *earn* the money, even if you don’t receive it until later. | In the year you *incur* the expense, even if you don’t pay it until later. | It matches income with the related costs, giving a clearer picture of profitability in the period in which the activity happens. |

**Examples**

*Cash method*: You invoice a client in December, but they pay in January. Under cash accounting you add that $1,000 to your 2025 income, because you *received* it in 2025. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

*Accrual method*: The same invoice is under accrual. You add the $1,000 to 2025 income because the sale was earned in 2025, even though the money comes in 2026. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

**Constructive receipt rule (cash method)**  
If money is credited to your account or made available to you without restriction, you are deemed to have received it for tax purposes, even if you don’t physically take it out. For example, interest credited in December 2025 is included in 2025 income if you haven’t withdrawn it. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**When you need accrual**

If your business holds inventory (goods on hand for sale, raw materials, or supplies that become part of merchandise) you normally must use the accrual method, because the inventory costs must be matched to the revenue they help generate. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

---

**Bottom line:**  
- **Cash** = “when the cash hits the bank.”  
- **Accrual** = “when the economic activity happens.”  

Choose the method that best reflects the timing of where your business’s money is actually earned and spent. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes. The IRS allows a taxpayer to deduct many ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while traveling on business, including

* **Travel costs** – airfare, train, bus, or car trips between your home and a temporary work location are deductible. You can deduct the full amount for flights, trains, buses, or for the actual car expenses (or the standard mileage rate). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
* **Transportation while on the trip** – taxi, commuter bus, limousine fares, parking and tolls between the airport or station and your hotel or between the hotel and your work site are deductible. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
* **Lodging** – the cost of hotel rooms is fully deductible when the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep to perform your duties. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Meals** – you may deduct the cost of meals (or a standard meal allowance) while traveling.  Generally only 50 % of the actual meal cost is deductible, unless you elect to take a standard meal allowance. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Other incidentals** – cleaning, telephone calls, and tips related to the trip are deductible. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

If you rent or own a vehicle and use it for the trip, you may deduct the business‑use portion of the operating expenses, or the standard mileage rate for business miles driven. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

Personal commuting—such as driving from your home to your regular place of business—is not deductible. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)  

For employee reimbursements, the deduction depends on whether the plan is accountable or non‑accountable; see Pub. 15 for guidance. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

In short, most ordinary and necessary travel expenses that are solely for business purposes can be deducted, subject to the limits above.

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is the first section of a business plan that gives a concise snapshot of the venture. According to the guidance in the context, it should:

1. Describe the core idea of the business.  
2. State how much capital is required, why the funding is needed, and what the money will be used for.  
3. Indicate how much equity or money the owners have already invested into the business.  
4. Provide a brief schedule of key milestones and goals.  
5. Be written **after** the rest of the plan is completed, so it can incorporate the most up‑to‑date information.  

These elements capture the essential information an executive summary is meant to convey. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the steps outlined in the plan template:

1. **Define your niche and best‑customer profile** – state the specific type of customer you aim to serve.  
   *Explain* why this group is the “best” for your product or service.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify key characteristics** – list the traits that describe these customers.  
   - For *consumer* markets: age, gender, income, lifestyle, geographic location, product use or benefits sought.  
   - For *business* markets: industry, company size, location, and how the product is used or applied.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment the market** – break the overall market into meaningful groups based on the characteristics above.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate size and growth potential** – use available data such as population figures, industry reports, or sales‑tax information to calculate the market’s approximate size.  
   *Project* how the market is expected to grow over time.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Project market capture** – indicate what portion of the total market you anticipate winning.  
   *Describe* the strategy or advantages that will allow you to reach that share.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), a business that serves the public must remove physical barriers that are “readily achievable” and provide at least one accessible entrance. If a barrier cannot be removed easily, the business must offer an alternative means of service or provide an accessible route elsewhere. Citations:

- The requirement to remove barriers: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) – “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable.”  
- The requirement for an accessible entrance: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) – “If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance … the alternative entrance must be open during store hours.”  
- If full accessibility is not practicable: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) – “... if it is not readily achievable to provide an accessible entrance, the goods and services must be provided in some other way, if doing so is readily achievable.”  

So, unless you can show that making a wheelchair‑accessible entrance or other required accommodations would be prohibitively difficult or expensive, you are required to make your shop wheelchair accessible or provide an alternative means of access.



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)
2. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You may be exempt from the regular OSHA injury‑recordkeeping forms if you meet **one** of the following conditions:

- **Your business had 10 or fewer workers during every month of the last calendar year** or 
- **You operate in a low‑hazard industry listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

In either case, you still **must** report the following to OSHA:

- Work‑related fatalities  
- In‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss‑of‑eye incidents [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

If your business had **100 or more workers** in a designated high‑hazard industry, you must submit copies of your OSHA Form 300 log and Form 301 incidents **electronically** by **March 2** of the year after the covered year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

All injury and illness records (Forms 300, 300A, and 301) must be kept on site for **at least five years** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

So, you are exempt from routine recordkeeping only under the two conditions above; otherwise, you must keep and report the required records.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
You must keep OSHA injury and illness records (Forms 300, 300A, and 301) at the worksite for **at least five years**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**What records you must keep**

| Record type | What to keep | How long to keep it |
|-------------|--------------|---------------------|
| **Tax records (income, deductions, credits, and related documents)** | Copies of filed tax returns; books and ledgers that support income, expenses, and credits; receipts, invoices, bank records, payroll records, etc. | Keep them for as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.  In practice this means: keep supporting documents until the period of limitations for that return expires, which is usually **4 years after the return is filed** unless a longer period applies. Also keep original returns.  If you have employees, keep employment‑tax records for **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid**.  Asset records (depreciation, basis, sale) must be kept until the limitations period expires for the year the property is disposed of.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** | Payroll books, W‑2s, W‑3s, 1099s, payroll tax returns (941/944, 940), etc. | Keep them for **4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid** (whichever is later).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Injury and illness records (OSHA)** | OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses), OSHA Form 301 (Incident Report for each recordable injury/illness), OSHA Form 300A (Annual Summary), worker medical and exposure records, and worker training records that must be available to employees. | *At the worksite*: keep injury/illness logs and incident reports for **at least 5 years**.  Medical and exposure records must be retained for the period required for each specific type of record, and training records must be kept and accessible as required by OSHA standards.  All required OSHA information must be electronically submitted on Form 300/301 annually by **March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered.  Fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye are reported to OSHA within 8 hours or 24 hours, respectively.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

**Key reminders**

* If you are a small business that also collects or pays taxes, the same **4‑year period** applies to employment‑tax records and varies for other tax items based on the specific deadlines and limitations in the tax code.  
* OSHA recordkeeping applies only if you have 10 or more workers in a high‑hazard industry, or if your industry requires detailed reporting; otherwise you may be exempt from keeping the logs for minor first‑aid injuries.  
* Always retain copies of the records that support your tax returns and injury reports in a form that the IRS or OSHA can review—paper or electronic with full retention and retrieval capabilities.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) (for electronic systems)  

These are the specific retention periods and record types given in the documents you provided.
