runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a legal form** – Decide whether you will operate as a *sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC*.  The type you pick determines the tax return you file and the record‑keeping rules you must follow.  See Segment 1 for the initial decision list and Segment 18 for filing requirements such as a fictitious name or articles of organization.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)*

2. **Get a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN)** – Even a sole proprietor or partnership needs an EIN if the business has employees, pays excise taxes, or prefers to keep the EIN for business use instead of a social‑security number.  It is obtained from the IRS.  See Segment 18.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)*

3. **Decide on a tax year and accounting method**  
   * *Tax year*: You may use a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or choose a fiscal year that ends on any month except December.  You must file Form 1128 if you want to change it later.  See Segments 1, 5, 30.  
   * *Accounting method*: Pick the “cash” or “accrual” method that best reflects your income and expenses.  The same method must be used for all tax returns and records.  See Segment 4 (and 1).  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)*

4. **Set up a separate business bank account and checkbook** – Keep business receipts and checks in the business account, not in your personal one.  Note the source of each deposit (income, personal loan, owner’s capital).  See Segments 10 and 7.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

5. **Keep good records** –  
   * Record every transaction as it occurs: sales, expenses, credit‑card or cash payments.  
   * Maintain a *daily* summary of cash receipts, a *monthly* summary of cash receipts, and a *check‑disbursements journal* (see Segments 10, 7).  
   * Keep supporting documents for every entry—receipts, invoices, credit‑card slips, bank statements.  Those documents should stay on hand in case the IRS requests them.  See Segments 2, 7, 10.  
   * Use either hard copy books (journals, ledgers) or a compliant electronic system that can index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce records in legible form.  See Segment 7.  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*

6. **Use the business checkbook for all business payouts** – Write checks payable to “you only” when withdrawing money for personal use, and avoid “cash” checks unless you attach a receipt or explanation.  See Segment 10.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

7. **Reconcile monthly** – Match the bank statement, your checkbook, and your books each month to catch errors early.  See Segment 10.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

8. **Track deductible expenses** – Ordinary and necessary expenses are deductible.  Record them promptly so nothing is omitted when you file.  See segments 6 and 34 for the definition and examples.  
   *[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)*

9. **File your tax returns**  
   * **Income tax** – A sole proprietor files a *Schedule C (Form 1040)* for each business.  For more than one business, attach separate Schedules C.  LLCs, corporations, and partnerships have their own forms.  See Segments 5, 12, 32.  
   * **Estimated tax** – If you expect to owe $1,000 or more, you must pay estimated tax quarterly using Form 1040‑ES.  Due dates are usually April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15 of the next year.  Pay electronically via EFTPS or Direct Pay.  See Segments 5, 20.  
   * **Other taxes** – If you have employees, file Forms 941, 940, W‑2/W‑3, 1099‑NEC, etc.  If you use certain equipment or goods, you may owe excise taxes on Forms 720 or 2290.  See Segments 13, 21, 25.  
   *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)*

10. **Deposit required taxes electronically** – All federal employment and excise taxes must be deposited via EFTPS.  A new EIN automatically enrolls the business in EFTPS, and the PIN is mailed in the PIN package.  See Segment 9.  
    *[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)*

11. **Keep records for IRS inspection** – Maintain all books and supporting documents on file for at least the length that the IRS requires (typically 3–7 years, depending on the tax type).  Keep them readily available for proof if the IRS audits you.  See Segments 2, 7.

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible, follow the specific requirements and recommendations found in the handbook’s safety and accessibility sections.  

---

### 1. Overall Safety Program  
- **Establish a Written Safety & Health Program.** The program should cover hazard identification, prevention, training, and continuous improvement. It must be reviewed at least annually. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)  
- **Implement Emergency Action Plans.** Identify evacuation conditions, assign responsibilities, and plan for people with disabilities or language barriers. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)  
- **Workplace Violence Prevention.** Put in place a written program, training, engineering controls (e.g., secure exits, panic buttons), and a “buddy system.” Keep records of incidents to identify trends. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=84)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=86)  
- **Lockout/Tagout Procedures.** Write procedures, train authorized workers, and lock out all stored energy before servicing machinery. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=49)  
- **Machinery & Equipment Safety.** Ensure equipment is anchored, guarded, and that operators have clear access to controls. Maintain equipment in good condition. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=53)  
- **Training and Supervision.** Provide job‑specific safety training, frequent refresher training, and supervise high‑risk tasks. Special attention should be paid to young workers (under 18) who cannot do hazardous work. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=88)[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=89)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=87)  
- **Regular Inspections and Hazard Removal.** Use a self‑inspection checklist to identify and eliminate hazards such as wet floors, blocked aisles, or unsafe ladders. [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

---

### 2. Accessible Entrance & Interior Access  
| Requirement | Detail | Source |
|-------------|--------|--------|
| **Accessible Entrance** | Provide a clearly marked, unobstructed path to at least one accessible entrance. If a door is locked for security, install an accessible call box or buzzer at no more than 48 in. above ground. The door must stay unlocked during business hours. | Segment 1, 17 |
| **Ramps** | Max slope 1:12. Handrails are required when slope >1:20 and rise >6 in. Width ≥ 36 in. | Segment 1, 4 |
| **If a ramp is not feasible** | Use a lift, platform lift, or folding lift that meets safety codes. | Segment 4 |
| **Turnstiles & Security Gates** | Remove or replace a narrow turnstile with an accessible gate or provide a separate accessible entrance. Minimum opening 32 in. Wide as possible. | Segment 2 |
| **Doors** | Minimum clear width 36 in. For older doors <36 in., consider widening or using a “swing‑clear” hinge. Replace tight‑grasp hardware (knobs, thumb latches) with lever handles or removable latches. | Segment 9 |

---

### 3. Parking & Route to the Store  
| Requirement | Detail | Source |
|-------------|--------|--------|
| **Accessible Parking** | 8‑ft wide spaces, 98‑in. vertical clearance. Provide at least one van‑accessible space; all others must be at way points. | Segment 3 |
| **Access Aisles** | Must be at least 8 ft wide for vans, 5 ft for cars, with a 1:50 slope maximum. | Segment 3, 11 |
| **Signage** | Use the international symbol of accessibility; mount so it cannot be hidden by parked vehicles. | Segment 3, 11 |
| **Crosswalks / Routes** | If the path from the parking lot to the entrance crosses vehicular traffic, mark and provide a safe route. | Segment 3 |

---

### 4. Interior Walkways & Work Areas  
- **Clearings & Pathways** – Keep walkways clean, free of debris, and well lit. Avoid obstructions. Provide 36‑in. minimum clear width for aisles, or 48‑in. width for 180° turns. [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
- **Elevated Surfaces & Tools** – Guard edges, install handrails, and keep head‑room requirements. Use guardrails or fall protection for surfaces >4 ft. [[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)[[19]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=74)  
- **Floor Holes** – Cover or guard all holes; use toeboards around edges. [[19]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=74)  
- **Ladders** – Maintain good condition, secure on all sides, and use only if the top is at least 3 ft above the surface. Use three‑point contact and do not carry items that could cause slipping. [[20]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=75)  

---

### 5. Accessible Counter & Service Areas  
- **Sales & Service Counters** – Maximum 36‑in. high with a clear 30 × 48‑in. floor space in front. Provide a lowered section of counter 60 in. long and no higher than 34 in. If not possible, provide service at an accessible table or via an alternative service. [[21]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[22]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Accessible Seating** – Fixed tables must have at least 27‑in. leg clearance and a 30 × 48‑in. clear floor space. At least 5 % of tables should be accessible. [[23]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  
- **Employee Service Areas** – Have a 36‑in. wide accessible checkout aisle for each checkout, with a sign marked “accessibility.” [[21]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  

---

### 6. Policies & Communication  
- **Update Policies** to remove barriers and allow service‑animal access, keep accessible entrances unlocked, and provide alternative service options if a physical barrier cannot be removed. [[24]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)  
- **Communication with Customers** – Use simple written notes or assistive devices for customers with hearing or speech disabilities. [[24]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)  
- **Signage** – Install the International symbol of accessibility on all accessible parking spaces and entrances. [[25]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[26]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)  

---

### 7. Training & Record‑Keeping  
- **Staff Training** – Cover hazard recognition, emergency procedures, first aid, lockout/tagout, ladder safety, and handling of workplace violence. Provide ongoing refresher training. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=88)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)[[27]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  
- **Record‑Keeping** – Track incidents (OSHA 300 log), near‑misses, and any injury. Review records annually to identify trends. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)  

---

### 8

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
To answer your request, the context segments **do cover both how to write a business plan and how to set up accounting**. Below is a step‑by‑step guide that pulls together the key points from the segments, using the requested citation format.

---

## 1. Writing a Business Plan

| Step | What to Include | Where the Guidance Comes From |
|------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Cover Page** | Company name, address, phone, owners, date, logo (if any). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Table of Contents** | Optional, but helps readers find sections quickly. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Executive Summary** | One‑two paragraphs summarizing the business idea, required capital, use of funds, and key milestones. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) |
| **Business Description** | Industry background, mission, legal structure, history, and long‑term goals. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13) |
| **Products / Services** | Detailed description of what you sell, unique features, production or service process, research & development, and future plans. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12) |
| **Market Analysis** | Target market, size, growth, customer needs, and competition (direct/indirect). | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15) |
| **Marketing & Sales Strategy** | Pricing, promotion, distribution channels, sales forecast, and customer acquisition plan. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) |
| **Operations Plan** | Location, facilities, equipment, inventory (inventory‑related guidance in [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) and [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)), suppliers, and key processes. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Management & Personnel** | Organizational structure, owners’ roles, key hires, and consulting partners. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13) |
| **Financial Plan** |  
- **Historical Financials** (if any)  
- **Projections** (3‑year income statement, cash‑flow, balance sheet) – include monthly projections for Year 1. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) |
| **Funding Request** | Total capital needed, use of funds, equity contribution, and repayment schedule. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16) |
| **Appendix** | Sample contracts, leases, CVs, permits, etc. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

> **Tips:**  
> *Write the Executive Summary last after the rest of the plan is complete.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
> *Use the “Notes and Critical Assumptions” page to explain the logic behind revenue and expense assumptions.* [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
> *Aim for a clear, paper‑size format unless you’re submitting electronically.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

---

## 2. Setting Up Accounting

### 2.1 Choose Your Business Structure & Tax ID
| Action | Guidance |
|--------|----------|
| Decide form of ownership (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation). | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3) |
| Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you have employees or prefer a business ID over your SSN. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |
| File any required “fictitious name” or “assumed business name” statements per state rules. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |

### 2.2 Pick an Accounting Method
| Method | When to Use | Instructions |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| **Cash method** | If you’re a small business that doesn’t keep inventory or only uses a simple book‑keeping system. | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Accrual method** | If you keep inventory or want a more detailed picture of income/expenses. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Combination method** | Treat it as cash if it includes cash. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

> **Tip:** Once chosen, you must use the same method for both tax and book‑keeping. Changing it later requires IRS Form 3115. [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

### 2.3 Open a Dedicated Business Bank Account
| Reason | Guidance |
|--------|----------|
| Keeps business funds separate from personal funds, simplifying reconciliation. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |
| Use the checkbook to record daily receipts and disbursements, noting each source. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |

### 2.4 Recordkeeping & Book‑keeping System
| Step | Details | Source |
|------|---------|--------|
| **Daily receipts** | Log every cash or check receipt immediately. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Check disbursements journal** | Record every check drawn, number, payee, and purpose. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Journal & Ledger** | For double‑entry bookkeeping: post each journal entry to the correct general ledger account. | [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you should track for taxes**

| Item | Why it matters (what you’ll report) | Where the guidance lives |
|------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **All income received** – including cash, checks, credit‑card sales, and non‑cash payments | Forms 1040‑ES, 1099‑MISC, 1099‑NEC, 1099‑B (and any other required information returns) need a dollar amount for the tax year. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Business expenses that are ordinary & necessary** – e.g., rent, utilities, supplies, phone, insurance, advertising, depreciation, bad debts, and any “other” deductible expense | These reduce taxable income on Schedule C (or the appropriate business return). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32) |
| **Deductible vehicle expenses** – mileage, fuel, maintenance, and depreciation for business use | You must split personal/​business mileage and keep a mileage log (at least a date‑by‑date log). | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36) |
| **Home‑office deduction** – if you qualify | Keeps track of the percent of the home used exclusively for business. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=2) |
| **Payroll‑related amounts** – gross wages, FICA, federal/state withholding, payroll taxes | Required on Forms W‑2, W‑3, and to compute your payroll tax liability. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Excise and fuel taxes** – if you owe any (e.g., heavy‑truck tax, fuel tax, environmental ect.) | You’ll file Form 720 or Form 2290, etc. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Estimated‑tax payments** – made quarterly when $1,000+ is owed (or $500+ for corporations) | Records each payment and the date, to avoid penalties. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |

**What you should track for travel expenses**

| Type | What to record | How to substantiate | Source |
|------|---------------|---------------------|--------|
| **Dates, destinations, purpose and business meetings** | “Business trip to Denver to meet client X June 12‑14” | Log in a travel journal or spreadsheet with a note of the business purpose. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Mileage & vehicle usage** | – Business miles driven, any tolls | Use a mileage log or a smartphone app that captures date, start/​end odometer, and purpose. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36) |
| **Transportation costs** | Flights, trains, taxis, car‑rental, ride‑share | Keep the receipt or ticket showing the date, amount, and traveler. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging (hotel, AirBnB, etc.)** | Night(s) stayed, location, cost | Keep the invoice or receipt; note if it was truly overnight and required rest. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Meals** | Cost of meals while traveling | Keep the receipt; if using the standard allowance, note the number of meals and the allowance rate. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Other business‑related costs** | Parking, tips, internet, business phone calls | Keep receipts or a log of the specific expense item, amount, and date. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Reimbursement records (if you pay employees)** | Amount reimbursed, how it was paid (accountable/non‑accountable plan) | Document the plan type and amount to deduct the reimbursement. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
You need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if your business:  
- Pays wages to one or more employees, or  
- Files pension or excise tax returns.  
A sole proprietor who does not have employees may still opt for an EIN to use instead of a social‑security number for the business. You can obtain an EIN online, by telephone, or by mailing/faxing Form SS‑4.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

**What accounting method comes with an EIN?**  
An EIN does not determine which accounting method you must use. The accounting method—either cash, accrual, or a special/combine method—is chosen by you when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (or equivalent). You may use the method that best fits your business. If you keep inventory you are generally required to use an accrual method for purchases and sales; otherwise a cash method is usually acceptable.  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
The OSHA record‑keeping rules require you to keep the following injury and illness records:

* **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** for each recordable injury or illness that occurs.  
* **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** (or an equivalent form that contains the same information) for each recordable case.  
* An **annual summary** prepared at the end of each calendar year using **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses**.  

These forms are to be retained at the worksite for **at least five years** from the date of the injury or illness.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
Yes. In most states you are required to carry workers’ compensation insurance for employees – it is set by state law to cover injuries or illnesses that happen on the job, regardless of fault. According to the information in the context, that insurance is also a deductible business expense: you can deduct the premiums you pay for workers’ compensation insurance on your Schedule C as an ordinary and necessary business cost.

runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
You need to file *both* federal employment‑tax forms and state‑specific employment‑tax paperwork.

| **What you file** | **Federal form(s)** | **State‐related requirement** | **Where it comes from** |
|-------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Pay‑and tax statements for employees** | *Form W‑2*, W‑3 (to report wages, tips, withholding, Social‑Security and Medicare taxes) | Submit W‑2/W‑3 to the IRS and give each employee a copy; remit state income‑tax withholdings to the state tax agency (the amount you collect from each employee is a state tax you owe and must report/​pay) | Segment 4, 11 |
| **Quarterly/fiscal‑year FICA & withholding returns** | *Form 941* (quarterly) or *Form 944* (annual) – reports Social Security, Medicare, federal income tax withholding | None at the federal level; the federal forms cover the employer’s share of FICA taxes | Segment 1 |
| **Federal unemployment tax (FUTA)** | *Form 940* – carried out every year | None – FUTA is federal only | Segment 1 |
| **State unemployment insurance (SUI)** | None federal; you must file a separate state unemployment‑insurance return each quarter | *Quarterly contributions* to the state’s unemployment‑insurance fund (payable to the state Dept. of Labor) | Segment 9 |
| **Other state‑level employee‑related taxes** | *State income‑tax withholding* – you must remit the amount you collect from employees to the state tax agency on a regular basis (usually monthly or quarterly, depending on the state) | None specified in the segments beyond the unemployment‑insurance requirement | Segment 9 |

---

### Key Points

1. **Federal FICA & withholding** – File *Form 941* (or *944*, if you qualify) each quarter/year to report the employee and employer portions of Social Security and Medicare taxes, plus the federal income tax you withheld. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  

2. **Federal unemployment (FUTA)** – File *Form 940* annually. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  

3. **Employee wage statements** – File *Form W‑2* (and *W‑3* transmittal) to report each employee’s wages and taxes paid. Provide a copy to each employee. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  

4. **State unemployment insurance (SUI)** – Pay quarterly contributions to the state unemployment‑insurance fund. In South Dakota, employers make these payments to the Dept. of Labor and must report new hires within 20 days. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)  

5. **State income‑tax withholding** – The payroll amounts you withhold for state income tax are a state tax you owe; they must be remitted to the state’s tax agency according to that state’s schedule. This is an ongoing requirement that follows the same logic as the federal withholding report. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)  

---

> **Bottom line** – For each employee you file **W‑2/W‑3**, **941/944**, and **940** at the federal level, and **quarterly state unemployment** contributions (and state withholding remittances) at the state level.  
> 
> If you need specific forms or due‑dates for your own state, consult the state tax agency’s website or the published schedules in *Pub. 509* (Tax Calendars).



**Sources:**

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through your front door**

- Make the entrance wide enough: older doors that are less than 36 in‑wide should be widened so the clear width when fully open is at least 32 inches. If a door is narrower, add “swing‑clear” hinges or install a lever handle to give the extra clearance.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
- Replace inaccessible hardware (e.g., round knobs or thumb‑latch handles that require a tight grasp) with a lever or a clamp‑on lever.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
- If a turnstile is blocking the entrance, remove it and keep the opening at least 32 inches wide, or, if that is not readily achievable, add an accessible gate adjacent to it.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
- When an entrance is inaccessible and another entrance is usable, mark that second entrance with a sign that indicates it is the accessible entrance and keep it open during business hours.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
- Provide a ramp, short wheelchair‑accessible walkway, or a lift if the entrance has a step or other barrier that prevents access. The ramp slope must not exceed 1:12 and the ramp width must be at least 36 inches. The landing beyond the door should extend at least 18 inches past the edge of the door.  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  
- In all cases, removing the barrier is an ongoing obligation: any barrier that is “readily achievable” to remove must be removed as resources allow.  
  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
- If you cannot modify the existing door, consider an alternative entrance that meets the width and accessibility standards and provide clear signage.  
  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

**If someone is hurt on site**

- Administer first aid immediately and, if the injury is more serious than a minor cut or bruise that requires only first aid, seek emergency medical assistance.  
  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=63)  
- Record the incident on OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) and then log it on OSHA Form 300 (Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) if it is a recordable injury (i.e., it requires medical treatment, results in days away from work, or is a death). Minor injuries that need only first aid are not required to be logged.  
  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
- Keep an annual summary on OSHA Form 300A by the end of each calendar year.  
  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
- Post emergency phone numbers where they can be found in case of another incident.  
  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)  
- Ensure your business has a safety and health program that includes procedures for reporting injuries, training workers on hazard identification, and maintaining a culture where workers are encouraged to report incidents and near‑misses.

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
You must meet two separate legal requirements:

| What you’re asking | Legal requirement | Source |
|------------------|------------------|--------|
| **Cash threshold for reporting** | If you receive **more than $10,000 in cash in one transaction, or in two or more related business transactions in a single day**, you must file IRS **Form 8300, Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000 Received in a Trade or Business**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **License to serve food** | Any business that **prepares and serves food** must first pass a health‑department inspection and obtain a **food license (or lodging license if the location also provides lodging)** before beginning operations. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8) |

**Key points**

* **Cash reporting** – The threshold applies to U.S. and foreign coin, currency, and certain monetary instruments such as cashier’s and traveler’s checks and money orders, but not to a personal check drawn on an individual’s account. Failure to file Form 8300 can lead to civil or criminal penalties, including up to 5 years’ imprisonment.  
* **Food‑service license** – The Health Department must approve the license after a complete inspection. Contact the department (e.g., (605) 773‑3361 in South Dakota) for application instructions.  

So, report cash payments over $10,000 and obtain the required health‑department food licence before serving.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark you can do it either at the state level or the federal level.  
1. **Decide where to register** – state registration gives you exclusive rights only within that state, while federal registration (through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office) gives you nationwide protection.  
2. **Search the databases first** to make sure the mark you want isn’t already taken. Use the state‑level database (if you’re filing in a state) or the federal USPTO Trademark Search System.  
3. **File the application**  
   * **State level** – file with your state’s Secretary of State office. For South Dakota you can contact the Secretary of State at (605) 773‑2797 or visit https://sdsos.gov/ [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10).  
   * **Federal level** – file through the USPTO. Complete the application online at www.uspto.gov, and if you need help, call (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)  
4. **Pay the required fee** (the amount depends on the type of application and the number of classes of goods/services).  
5. **Wait for examination** – the USPTO will review your application and may issue an Office Action requesting changes or a refusal. Respond promptly to keep the application moving.  
6. **Receive registration** – once the USPTO approves, you’ll receive a registration certificate that grants you exclusive rights nationwide.  

These steps cover when you’ll register, whom to contact, and where to file. If you choose a state filing, the Secretary of State will also provide local instructions and filing forms. If you go federal, the USPTO website and contacts give all the details for completing the online application.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
Keep the documentation that backs up each item on your tax return until the time the IRS can still consider it relevant.  
* For most returns, that means keeping the records that support each income or deduction until the **period of limitations** for that return expires [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* If you have employees, you must keep every employment‑tax record for at least **four (4) years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* For property, keep the records relating to the asset until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable transaction [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* Always retain copies of the tax returns you file, as they are useful for future filings and for the IRS to review [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several essential purposes that help you run, grow, and protect your business:

1. **Monitor the progress of your business.**  
   Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which products sell best, and what changes are needed.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **Prepare accurate financial statements.**  
   Records are needed to create income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which you may need when dealing with banks, creditors, or for internal management.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Identify the source of receipts.**  
   Record where money or property comes from so you can separate business from non‑business receipts and distinguish taxable from nontaxable income.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Track deductible expenses.**  
   You could forget an expense unless you record it when it occurs; accurate records help claim all allowable deductions.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Prepare tax returns.**  
   Records support the income, expenses, and credits reported on your tax returns. The IRS may request them for inspection, so having a complete set speeds up any examination.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

6. **Support items reported on tax returns.**  
   Keep records available at all times for IRS inspection; a complete set clarifies items that the IRS may question.  
   → [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

In addition, the IRS requires that all records needed for tax purposes be retained. They must be kept as long as they are material to the administration of tax law and must be documented in an accessible format, whether in hard copy or electronic form.  
→ [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

Thus, keeping thorough business records is vital for monitoring operations, producing financial statements, meeting tax obligations, and safeguarding against audits.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the steps below. These are drawn directly from the handbook’s guidance and the resources it recommends.

1. **Plan a routine self‑inspection**  
   • Choose a knowledgeable, experienced worker (or team) to lead the inspection.  
   • Schedule inspections regularly so you can spot new or changing hazards before they cause problems.  
   • During each visit, identify hazards, apply or update controls, and verify that the controls remain effective.  
   ["An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections" – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)].

2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists**  
   • The handbook supplies checklists for general‑industry workplaces.  
   • Start by walking through the entire work area and tick off each potential hazard listed.  
   • The checklists also provide notes on what to do next and links to extra resources.  
   ["The checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)].

3. **Compile and analyze the information**  
   • After you finish a checklist, gather data on injuries, illness records, worker training, maintenance logs, and any failure or incident reports.  
   • Look for patterns that point to recurring problems or missing controls.  
   • Use OSHA standards and other resources cited in the handbook to find solutions.  
   ["Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information… to help you determine where challenges exist” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)].

4. **Seek outside help if needed**  
   • If you’re unsure whether a particular standard applies or how to implement a control, consult OSHA’s website, local Office of Management or the nearest On‑Site Consultation program.  
   • The On‑Site Consultation program offers free, confidential visits that can focus on a single concern or a full‑facility hazard assessment.  
   ["Consultants from OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation programs… can help small business employers with this process at no cost" – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)];  
   ["If you have any questions… visit the OSHA website or contact the nearest OSHA Area Office or your state On‑Site Consultation program" – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)].

5. **Document everything**  
   • Keep a written record of each inspection, the hazards found, the controls applied, and any follow‑up actions taken.  
   • These records help you track progress and demonstrate due diligence.  

By combining regular self‑inspections, the handbook’s checklists, supporting OSHA records, and optional expert consultation, you create a repeatable, evidence‑based process for identifying and eliminating workplace hazards.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting records money when it actually moves in and out of your bank account, whereas accrual‑method accounting records money when it is earned or spent, regardless of when the dollars change hands.  

- **Cash method**: Income is reported in the tax year you receive it; expenses are generally deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
- **Accrual method**: Income is reported in the year it is earned (even if payment comes later); expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, whether or not you have paid them yet. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

Because inventory balances must reflect the cost of goods available for sale, businesses that maintain inventory are generally required to use the accrual method for purchases and sales. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

A short example: If you sell a computer on December 28, 2025, invoice it in early January 2026, and receive payment in February 2026, a cash‑method taxpayer would report the income only when the cash is received, but an accrual‑method taxpayer would include the sale income in 2025. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – you can deduct a wide range of costs that are reasonable and necessary for a business trip.  The tax rules let you take a deduction for the **transportation** to and from the business destination, for **overnight meals and lodging**, for **baggage shipping or sample transport**, and for any **local transportation** you use while away from home.  The deduction rules are set out in the publication excerpts below:

| Expense type | Deductible? | How the deduction is calculated | Key limits or requirements |
|--------------|-------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Airplane, train, bus, or car travel** between your home and the business destination | **Yes** | Deduct the full amount you pay for tickets or the business‑use portion of a rental or personal vehicle. | Must be between your home (or “tax home”) and the temporary work location, and the trip must be primarily for business. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine, or other local transport** between the airport or station, your hotel, and the work site | **Yes** | Deduct the fare or equivalent fee. | Same “between home and destination” rule applies. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Baggage, samples, or display material shipping** between regular and temporary work sites | **Yes** | Deduct the shipping cost. | Must be for business purposes. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Rental car, own car, van, or truck use while away** | **Yes** | Deduct the business‑use portion of the rental fee, or you may use actual vehicle operating expenses (e.g., gas, tolls, parking) or the standard mileage rate. | If you use the vehicle for both personal and business purposes, allocate expenses based on business miles. (See also Segment 5.) |
| **Meals** | **Yes, but partially** | You may deduct  **50 %** of your actual meal expenses, or you may use the standard meal allowance (different rates apply each year). | Only if the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep or rest to perform your duties; whether you use the 50 % rule or the standard allowance is up to you. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging (hotel, motel, etc.)** | **Yes** | Deduct the full cost of the overnight stay. | Must meet the same overnight/“need sleep” rule as for meals. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Cleaning (dry‑cleaning, laundry)** | **Yes** | Deduct the cost of cleaning services performed while you are traveling. | Only during the business trip. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Telephone or other communication costs** | **Yes** | Deduct business‑use calls, fax, or other communications made while traveling. | Only the business portion. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips** | **Yes** | Deduct tips you pay for services listed above (e.g., hotel, taxi, meals). | Only the business‑related tips. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Reimbursement to employees** | **Yes (generally)** | If you reimburse employees for their travel and meal expenses, the amount is deductible to the business. How you deduct it depends on whether the reimbursement falls under an accountable or non‑accountable plan. | Follow Pub. 15 for details. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

### Summary

* You **can** deduct ordinary and necessary travel expenses that are directly tied to a business trip.
* **Transportation** (air, rail, bus, car, local taxi) between your **home** and a temporary work location is fully deductible.
* **Meals** are deductible at **50 %** of the cost (or a standard allowance if you use that method).
* **Lodging** is fully deductible, but only for overnight or “long‑duration” trips that require sleep or rest.
* **Other incidental expenses** such as cleaning, telephone calls, baggage shipping, and tips are also deductible, but only the business portion.

So, if your trip meets the “overnight or long enough to need sleep” requirement, you can deduct a large portion of your travel-related costs—just be sure to keep records that separate the business portion from any personal use.

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
In a business plan, the executive summary is a brief overview that gives readers a quick understanding of the business and its goals. It usually includes:

- **A concise description of the business idea** – what the business does and its value proposition.  
- **The amount of funding needed** – how much money you are seeking and what it will be used for.  
- **Sources of capital** – what money you have already invested (or plan to invest) and any other capital commitments.  
- **A brief schedule of key milestones** – important future goals and projected timelines.  

This section is typically one or two paragraphs, so it is written last after the rest of the plan is completed. It should give the reader a quick snapshot before they read the detailed sections. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the guidance in the plan template:

1. **Define the niche you serve** – state the specific market segment that is most likely to buy your product or service.  
   – *Describe who your best customer is.*  
   – Identify those customers and “describe their characteristics.”  
   – In a B2B context you might classify the market by industry, company size, location, or product use/application; in a consumer context you can segment by age, gender, income, lifestyle, geographic location, or benefits sought.  

   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Estimate market size and growth potential** – use population data, industry reports, sales‑tax information or other relevant statistics.  
   – Estimate how much of the total market you expect to capture.  

   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Tie the description to your marketing plan** – once you know who your target customers are, you can tailor your promotion, distribution and location choices to match their preferences and behaviour.  

   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

In short, *describe the niche, list the key characteristics of the customers who belong there, and provide an estimate of the market’s size and your expected share*. This creates a clear, data‑backed picture of the people (or businesses) you’re aiming to reach.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  Because your shop serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove “barriers that are readily achievable” and to provide accessible routes, entrances, parking, and service areas.  The key points are:

| Requirement | What you must do | Where it is found |
|-------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Accessible entrance** | If the shop has more than one public entrance, at least one must be accessible.  If one entrance is not accessible but another is, a sign must direct customers to the accessible one, and the alternative entrance must be open during hours. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Entrance design** | The accessible entrance must include a ramp (max slope 1:12) or other means to remove steps, a landing wide enough for a 90° turn, handrails, and an accessible route that is steps‑free, slip‑resistant, and firm. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Accessible parking** | Provide at least one accessible parking space for every 25 spaces (two for 50 or fewer) and make the space adjacent to the accessible entrance, with a 5‑ft (for cars) or 8‑ft (for vans) access aisle, and a clear vertical clearance of at least 98 inches. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Accessible service areas** | All counters that sell or serve customers must have an accessible section no higher than 34 in.  If that is not readily achievable, a nearby accessible table or an assistant can provide service. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Internal routes and aisles** | Provide a 36‑in. wide accessible route between displays, shelves, and directly to service areas, with 3‑ft turning spaces and a 60‑in. diameter turn if a 180° turn is needed. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Ongoing obligation** | Improvely that are “readily achievable” must be made, but changes that would be excessive in cost or difficulty may be deferred. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) |

In short, you are required to **make your shop wheelchair‑accessible** to the extent that such improvements are *readily achievable* under the ADA.  If certain changes are not readily achievable (e.g., your building layout prohibits a ramp or adequate parking), you must provide comparable services elsewhere or give alternative ways to obtain goods and services.

runs.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
runs.answer:
You must report a workplace death to OSHA within **8 hours** of the incident.  

- OSHA requires that all work‑related fatalities be reported within 8 hours [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
- For fatalities involving infectious diseases, the same 8‑hour deadline applies [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48).

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness **recordkeeping** (OSHA Forms 300, 301 and 300A) only under specific circumstances mentioned in OSHA regulation 29 CFR 1904.1 and its subparts:

- **If you had 10 or fewer employees during every day of the last calendar year** – then you are partially exempt from recording non‑fatal injuries and illnesses.  
- **If your business is in one of the low‑hazard industries listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A** – then you are also exempt from recording.

Even if exempt, you must still **report** to OSHA:

- All work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye within 8 hours (fatalities) and 24 hours (hospitalizations, amputations, eye loss). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

If you do *not* meet either of those exemption criteria, you must maintain OSHA injury and illness records.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
You must keep OSHA injury and illness records (Forms 300, 300A, and 301) at the worksite for **at least five years**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**What you must keep for tax purposes**

| Type of record | Why you need it | How long you must keep it (IRS rules) |
|----------------|-----------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Documents that support every item of income or deduction on a tax return** (e.g., invoices, receipts, bank statements, payroll records) | They back up what you report on your return so you can argue the amounts if the IRS questions you. | Keep them until **the “period of limitations”** for that return runs out – the IRS can only change your tax for the years that are still within the limitations period. This period is usually **up to 4 years** for most returns, but it can vary depending on the type of tax. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Copies of the tax returns you filed** | They help you prepare future returns and are evidence of what you reported. | Keep them for the same period as the supporting records (commonly 4 years). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (payslips, W‑2s, Form 941/944, payroll tax deposits, etc.) | They show the wages you paid and the taxes you withheld/deposited. | Keep them **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid (whichever is later)**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Asset‑related records** (purchase invoices, sales receipts, depreciation schedules, cost‑basis statements, etc.) | Needed to calculate gains, losses, depreciation and basis when the asset is sold or disposed of. | Keep them **until the limitations period for the year you dispose of the property** expires. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Other supporting documents** such as petty‑cash slips, inventory lists, expense reports, and written agreements | They support specific deductions or business expenses. | Keep them for the same time as the rest of your tax‑related records – usually **4 years, until the limitations period ends**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

> **Key term** – **Period of limitations**: the maximum time the IRS can change your tax liability. For ordinary income tax returns it is usually 3 to 4 years after the return is filed, but the IRS may allow more time for certain situations.

---

**What you must keep for injuries / OSHA records**

| Record | What it captures | Minimum retention period | When you must report to OSHA |
|--------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Main log of each recordable injury or illness. | **At least 5 years** at the worksite, even if you fire or close the business. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report | Detailed follow‑up on each Form 300 case. | Also kept for **5 years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A** – Annual Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Yearly summary of all Form 300/301 entries. | Stored for **5 years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** (e.g., medical evaluations, exposure monitoring reports) | Evidence that you met health‑and‑safety requirements. | Retained for the **time required for each specific type of record** (e.g., medical records typically 5 years). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What to track for taxes**

| Item | Why it matters | Where it’s mentioned |
|------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Sales tax collected** – you must keep a record of the amount you collect from customers and turn over to the state; you cannot deduct it as income. | “You cannot take a deduction for sales tax turned over to the state because you only collected the tax.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Excise taxes** – any excise tax you pay on products, equipment, or services should be recorded, because it may be deductible or reported on a special return (Form 720, 2290, etc.). | “You can deduct all excise taxes that are ordinary and necessary… Use Form 720… Form 2290 for heavy trucks.” | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Fuel taxes** – the tax on gasoline or diesel is built into the fuel cost; record the gross fuel expense but not the tax separately. | “Taxes on gasoline … are usually included as part of the cost of the fuel. Don’t deduct these taxes as a separate item.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Employment taxes** – if you have employees you must record wages, tips, FICA, and FUTA taxes so they can be reported on Forms 941/940 and included in your total tax liability. | “Form 941, Employer’s Quarterly Federal Tax Return, or Form 944…” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Estimated tax payments** – if you expect to owe $1,000 or more when you file, record each quarterly payment so your year‑end tax return reflects what you’ve already paid. | “You generally have to make estimated tax payments if you expect to owe tax of $1,000 or more…” | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Record‑keeping of tax documents** – keep canceled checks, invoices, bank statements, and credit‑card slips that show the amount paid and the business purpose; these documents support the amounts you claim. | “Documents for expenses include the following: canceled checks, credit‑card slips, invoices…” | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

**What to track for travel expenses**

| Item | Why it matters | Where it’s mentioned |
|------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Business mileage** – log the total miles driven, the business portion, and the purpose of each trip so you can apply the standard mileage rate (or actual expenses). | “The standard mileage rate is a specified amount of money you can deduct for each business mile you drive.” | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Log of local transportation** – keep receipts for rides between workplaces in your tax‑home area. | “Local transportation expenses include the ordinary and necessary costs of getting from one workplace to another in the course of your business.” | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34) |
| **Meals** – keep separate receipts for meals taken while on business trips; you can deduct 50 % of the cost (or a standard allowance). | “You can deduct the cost of meals… In most cases, you can deduct only 50 % of your meal expenses.” | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging** – keep hotel or motel receipts; you may deduct 100 % if the trip is overnight or long enough to need rest. | “You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest.” | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Parking, tolls, and toll‑free lanes** – keep receipts; these are deductible (and may be deducted separately if you claimed mileage). | “You may be able to deduct business‑related parking fees, tolls, interest on your car loan, and certain state and local taxes.” | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |

| **Record-keeping for travel** – attach each petty‑cash slip or expense to the corresponding receipt; keep a log of all trips, including dates, destinations, and purpose. | “Specific record‑keeping rules apply to these expenses… See Pub. 463.” | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
Yes.

* **Do you need an EIN?**  
  * If you are a sole proprietor, partnership, corporation, or an LLC, the IRS gives you an EIN for tax filing and reporting purposes.  
  * An EIN is required if you:  
    * hire employees, or  
    * will pay federal excise or payroll taxes, or  
    * want to use a business identification number instead of your Social Security number.  
  This requirement is stated in the IRS guidance on taxpayer identification numbers and is reiterated in state guidance (e.g., South Dakota’s regulations).  

  *Sole‑proprietors who have no employees may still obtain an EIN if they choose; it is not strictly mandatory unless one of the above situations applies.*  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

* **What accounting method does an EIN “come with”?**  
  The accounting method you use is **not** determined by whether you have an EIN.  
  * You choose an accounting method (cash or accrual) when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C or equivalent.  
  * The IRS allows any of the basic methods—cash, accrual, or a combination—provided the method consistently shows your income and expenses for the tax year.  
  * The choice is independent of having an EIN; the EIN is only a taxpayer‑identification number.  

  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
**Forms you must keep for work‑related injuries**

| Form | What it records | Where it’s kept | How long to keep it |
|------|-----------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | A daily record of all recordable injuries and illnesses that occur in the workplace. | On the worksite (paper form) **or** electronically submitted to OSHA. | At least **five (5) years** after the date the record was created. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report | A detailed narrative of each recordable injury or illness (used only for “recordable” cases). | On the worksite or electronically submitted to OSHA. | At least **five (5) years** after the record was created. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Annual summary of the year‑long totals from the 300 and 301 logs. | On the worksite (paper) or electronically submitted to OSHA. | At least **five (5) years** after the year it covers. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

> **Additional notes**  
> • If you have **10 or fewer workers** or work in a low‑hazard industry, you may be **exempt** from some or all of these record‑keeping rules, but you still must report fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye within the required timeframes. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
> • **Worker medical and exposure records** (e.g., medical evaluations, test results) are kept **for the time period required for each specific type of record** – this can be longer than five years depending on the health condition. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**Bottom line**

- Keep **Forms 300, 301, and 300A** on hand at the workplace (or in an electronic system) for a minimum of **five years**.  
- Keep any detailed **medical or exposure records** for the length of time the law requires for that particular health condition.  

These provisions come from OSHA’s record‑keeping rules for work‑related injuries and illnesses.

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
Yes. Most states require employers who have employees to carry workers’‑compensation insurance to protect the workforce and to limit civil liability [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9). Because workers’‑comp insurance is a statutory payroll‑expense, the premiums you pay for it are treated as a deductible business expense and can be claimed on Schedule C (Form 1040) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37).

(Your state may also require state income‑tax withholding from employee wages, but the specific form numbers and filing deadlines are state‑dependent and are not listed in the supplied segments.)

**Summary**

- File **Form W‑2** and **Form W‑3** for every employee.
